what_its_for: Propranolol is used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), irregular heartbeats, tremors (shaking), migraines, and anxiety related to performance situations. It belongs to a group of medicines called beta-blockers, which work by slowing your heart rate and reducing the workload on your heart.
how_to_take: Take propranolol exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take regular tablets with or without food, but try to take them the same way each time (always with food or always without). Extended-release capsules (LA or XL) should be swallowed whole — do not crush, chew, or open them. Take your dose at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause serious heart problems.
dosing: Your dose depends on the condition being treated and your personal health needs. Doses typically range from 10 mg to 320 mg per day, taken in 1 to 4 divided doses depending on the form prescribed. Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly adjust it. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next regular dose. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store propranolol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children. Do not use it past the expiration date on the label. Dispose of unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking propranolol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and increase dizziness. Do not take cold, flu, or allergy medicines without checking with your pharmacist first, as some of these can raise your blood pressure or interfere with propranolol. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, since it can cause dizziness or drowsiness. Do not stop taking propranolol suddenly without your doctor's approval.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: very slow heartbeat (less than 50 beats per minute), severe dizziness or fainting, shortness of breath or wheezing, unusual weight gain or swelling in your legs or feet, cold or numb hands and feet, depression or mood changes, signs of low blood sugar if you are diabetic (since propranolol can hide these symptoms), or a skin rash. Seek emergency help immediately if you have chest pain, difficulty breathing, or signs of a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat.
when_it_works: For high blood pressure, propranolol may start to lower your blood pressure within a few hours, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks to feel the full benefit. For migraines and tremors, it may take several weeks to notice improvement. For chest pain or irregular heartbeat, effects may be noticed sooner. Even if you feel well, keep taking your medicine unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and low blood pressure, so extra caution is needed to prevent falls. Pregnant women should only use propranolol if clearly needed, as it may affect the baby's heart rate and growth — tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Propranolol passes into breast milk, so talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. People with asthma, COPD, diabetes, or kidney or liver problems should inform their doctor before taking this medicine, as special monitoring or dose adjustments may be needed.
